stem: Harry is a two-year-old boy with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, mild coryzal symptoms, intercostal/subcostal recessions, and oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. Which of the following would you include in his initial management?

options.text: Oxygen via mask, nebulised salbutamol and oral dexamethasone
Oxygen via mask, nebulised adrenaline and oral dexamethasone
IM adrenaline, oral dexamethasone, and nebulised salbutamol
Oxygen via mask and oral dexamethasone

explanation: This child has moderate croup with stridor at rest. Initial management includes keeping the child calm, giving corticosteroid (dexamethasone), and nebulised adrenaline for moderate to severe symptoms. Salbutamol is not useful in croup because the problem is upper airway oedema, not lower airway bronchospasm.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The vignette is classic croup with stridor at rest and respiratory distress. The best answer among the existing options is nebulised adrenaline plus oral dexamethasone.

optionExplanations.A: Salbutamol does not treat upper airway obstruction in croup.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: nebulised adrenaline and dexamethasone are appropriate for moderate croup; oxygen may also be given if needed.
optionExplanations.C: IM adrenaline is not the standard treatment here, and salbutamol is not indicated.
optionExplanations.D: Dexamethasone alone is insufficient for moderate croup with stridor at rest.
optionExplanations.E: Salbutamol is not effective for croup.

Clinical scenario 3 - Harry

Harry, a two year old boy, presents with a barking cough and stridor at rest. He had been well up until this evening, apart from a mild runny nose and slight cough. On examination he has moderate respiratory distress with intercostal and subcostal recessions and tug. His RR is 35, HR 140 and saturations 94% in room air. He has a clear chest and inspiratory stridor at rest. He has been previously well and his immunisations are up to date.

The following five questions refer to Harry's clinical scenario.
